newsitem.title: FRANCE: "Fifth Element" boosts Gaumont results in France.
newsitem.headline: "Fifth Element" boosts Gaumont results in France.

text.p: Gaumont, the French film production and distribution company, said the success of Luc Besson's film, "The Fifth Element", pushed turnover at its film-making division above that of its distribution arm for the first time ever.

It said in a statement on Monday about its first half results that the film, which was premiered at the Cannes film festival last spring, accounted for turnover of 535 million francs ($86.3 million) up to June 30, of which 443 million was made outside France.
The film is "to date released in about 30 countries where, with hardly an exception, it has topped box office entries at least for the first two weeks of its release", Gaumont said.
"It has been seen by 35 million spectators, of whom a third were in the United States and over 6.7 million in France," it said.

Overall Gaumont posted a 43-percent rise in net attributable profit to 48.2 million francs for the six months to June 30, on turnover 87 percent higher than in 1996's first half at 1.17 billion francs.
Operating profit rose 78 percent to 101.1 million francs. The net attributable profit figure includes a rise of 15 percent in company taxes recently announced by the government.
The company's film-making turnover rose to 680.7 million francs from 235.2 million in the 1996 period.

Gaumont said two other films, "Amour et Confusions" (Love and Confusion) by Patrick Braoude and "Les Soeurs Soleil" (The Sun Sisters) by Jeannot Szwarc, had produced disappointing results. It gave no figures.
Gaumont gave no forecast for the full year, but said Gerard Krawcwyk's "Heroines" and Ariel Zeitoun's "XXL" would be key in its second half.
The shooting of "Visiteurs II", by Jean-Marie Poire and

Christian Clavier, a sequel to the successful 1994 mediaeval time-travel comedy "Les Visiteurs" (the Visitors), has been completed but the film will not be released until 1998, Gaumont said. WEM/SLA ($ = 6.196 French Francs)
